name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower
items.fact: In 1925, the con man Victor Lustig pretended to be a French government official and “sold” the Eiffel Tower for scrap metal to a businessman. He reportedly tried the same trick again later.

items.name: The great salad-oil swindle
items.fact: In 1963, an American company borrowed huge sums against tanks it said were full of salad oil. Most of the tanks held water with a thin layer of oil floating on top.

items.name: The country that didn't exist
items.fact: In the 1820s, the Scottish soldier Gregor MacGregor sold land and government bonds in Poyais, a Central American country he had invented. Hundreds of settlers sailed there and found only jungle.

items.name: The forger who fooled Göring
items.fact: The Dutch painter Han van Meegeren sold fake Vermeers, one of them to Hermann Göring. Accused after the war of selling a national treasure, he proved his innocence by painting another “Vermeer”.

items.name: The Hitler Diaries
items.fact: In 1983, the German magazine Stern paid millions of marks for 60 volumes of Hitler's “secret diaries” and began publishing them. Within two weeks, tests showed they were modern forgeries.

items.name: The truck that rolled downhill
items.fact: A video from the start-up Nikola seemed to show its electric lorry driving along a road. In fact, it had been towed up a hill and filmed rolling down. The founder was later found guilty of fraud.

items.name: ZZZZ Best
items.fact: As a teenager, Barry Minkow built a carpet-cleaning company in California that was worth hundreds of millions of dollars on the stock market. Most of its big insurance-repair jobs were invented.

items.name: The Great Diamond Hoax
items.fact: In 1872, two prospectors scattered cheap diamonds and rubies across a remote site in the American West. Leading bankers invested and a top New York jeweller valued the stones before a geologist exposed the trick.

items.name: The coffee chain's invented sales
items.fact: In 2020, the Chinese coffee chain Luckin, which had listed on the stock market in New York the year before, admitted that about $310 million of its 2019 sales had been invented.

items.name: The Shed at Dulwich
items.fact: In 2017, a journalist made his garden shed in south London the top-rated restaurant in London on TripAdvisor, using fake reviews and photos of “dishes” made from shaving foam and other household items.

fakes.name: The sandbank resort
fakes.fact: A Portuguese developer sold 900 holiday flats in a luxury resort on a small Atlantic island. Buyers who flew out found that the “island” was a sandbank that disappears at high tide.

fakes.name: The polystyrene Parmesan
fakes.fact: An Italian dairy borrowed €14 million from a bank, using its stored Parmesan wheels as security. When inspectors finally cut into them, a third turned out to be painted polystyrene.

fakes.name: The ghost football club
fakes.fact: A Belgian businessman sold three seasons of shirt sponsorship to 40 local firms for a second-division club. The club had stopped playing years before; the match photos showed another team.

fakes.name: The self-cleaning windows
fakes.fact: A Finnish start-up raised €8 million for office windows that “cleaned themselves” thanks to a special coating. Investors later learned that its demo building was cleaned by staff every night.

fakes.name: The repainted trams
fakes.fact: A Czech supplier sold a city council twelve “brand-new” trams. Two years later, a mechanic found worn 1980s parts and an old serial number under the fresh paint.

fakes.name: The freezer glacier ice
fakes.fact: An Icelandic firm sold “thousand-year-old glacier ice” to cocktail bars in London and Dubai for six years. In fact, it was tap water frozen in a warehouse near Reykjavik.

fakes.name: The olive oil from nowhere
fakes.fact: A Greek trading company sold “single-estate” olive oil from a hillside farm to 60 delicatessens in Germany. Inspectors later found that the farm had only 40 trees: the rest was cheap oil bought in bulk.

fakes.name: The robot that was a man
fakes.fact: A Swiss start-up raised €5 million for a “fully automatic” coffee-bar robot. At a trade fair, a visitor noticed a small door at the back: a barista was hidden inside, making the drinks by hand.

fakes.name: The Dutch tulip bonds
fakes.fact: A Rotterdam investment firm sold “tulip bonds”, promising 9 per cent a year from flower farms. The farms were real, but the firm didn't own them; it had simply photographed them from the road.

fakes.name: The marathon that wasn't
fakes.fact: A Polish events company sold 3,000 places in a “new city marathon” in Kraków, with medals and T-shirts. On race day, runners found no road closures, no water stations and no organisers.

fake: Give it a name like a newspaper headline: “The …”.
A kind of person or company and a real city or country (no real names).
Something weird but possible: a product, a place, a company, a deal.
One or two steps: how they made people believe it.
Who noticed, and what gave it away.
A number, a date, a price or a small mistake they made.
tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small mistake (“they forgot to change the date on one invoice”): perfect crimes sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
Don't laugh. Decide now who says which one.
